5 STEPS TO MANAGE AMAZON BEDROCK COSTS: BEYOND SIMPLY REDUCING TOKEN USAGE This article was shared with the AWS Study Group community.
Published post: View the article on Facebook
Article Content When deploying Generative AI applications with Amazon Bedrock, costs depend on more than token consumption and model pricing. Identifying cost sources, monitoring resource usage, and implementing appropriate controls are also essential.
An AWS Machine Learning Blog article introduces a five-step cost management approach to help organizations monitor, control, and optimize Amazon Bedrock expenses throughout application operations.
Key Takeaways 1. Attribute Costs: Use AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0), IAM tags, and AWS Cost Explorer to analyze spending across users, teams, or applications. 2. Monitor Usage: Enable Model Invocation Logging to track model invocations and analyze token consumption using Amazon CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3. 3. Enforce Budget Controls: Combine AWS Budgets for alerts, IAM and automation for access restrictions, or an application gateway to control requests before model invocation. 4. Optimize Costs: Use Intelligent Prompt Routing, Prompt Caching, and appropriate token limits to reduce unnecessary resource consumption. 5. Review and Improve: Monitor model usage, failed requests, and Prompt Caching effectiveness to continuously refine cost-management policies. Practical Applications This approach is useful for Generative AI applications that need to manage costs across multiple users, teams, or workloads, especially as request volumes and token consumption increase.
Instead of reviewing billing reports only at the end of each month, organizations can combine usage data, budget alerts, and optimization techniques to proactively manage Amazon Bedrock costs.

Summary Report: “GenAI-powered App & Database Modernization Workshop” Event Metadata Event Name: GenAI-powered App-DB Modernization Workshop Date & Time: August 13, 2025 | 09:00 – 17:00 Venue: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, District 1, Ho Chi Minh City Role: Attendee Keynote Speakers Jignesh Shah – Director, Open Source Databases at AWS Erica Liu – Senior GTM Specialist, App Modernization at AWS Fabrianne Effendi – Associate Specialist Solutions Architect, Serverless at AWS Executive Workshop Highlights 1. Identifying the Bottlenecks of Legacy Monoliths Delayed Time-to-Market: Tightly coupled codebases turn minor feature deployments into high-risk release events, dragging release cycles from weeks to months. Fragile Reliability: A bug in a single non-critical module (e.g. reporting) can bring down the entire transactional application. Operational Overhead: Difficulty scaling specific components independently leads to excessive cloud resource over-provisioning. 2. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) & Strategic Decomposition Event Storming Methodology: Mapping out real business processes chronologically through domain events before writing any code. Bounded Contexts: Defining clear, autonomous domain boundaries to isolate database ownership and API contracts. Context Mapping: Applying upstream/downstream integration patterns (Shared Kernel, Customer-Supplier, Anti-Corruption Layer). 3. Event-Driven Asynchronous Architectures Transitioning from synchronous REST API cascades to loose coupling powered by message buses (Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS/SQS). Comparing communication models: Publish/Subscribe, Point-to-Point, and Event Streaming. 4. Evolution of Serverless Compute Evaluating the compute spectrum: Virtual Machines (Amazon EC2) -> Containers (Amazon ECS/EKS) -> Serverless (AWS Fargate & AWS Lambda). How serverless eliminates operational undifferentiated heavy lifting, auto-scaling seamlessly with demand. 5. Accelerating Transformations with Amazon Q Developer Leveraging Generative AI directly within the IDE for code explanation, test generation, and automated Java 8 to Java 17/21 runtime upgrades. Using AI-assisted agents to refactor monolithic stored procedures into lightweight cloud-native microservices. Personal Reflections & Student Takeaways Business-First Architecture Mindset The workshop completely shifted my perspective: Good software architecture is never about picking the trendiest framework; it is about accurately modeling the business domain and building systems that adapt swiftly to business changes.
Practical Application to My Capstone Project Applied loose coupling to my proposal: Rather than having the ingestion backend write directly to multiple destinations synchronously, I integrated asynchronous event messaging. Started adopting Amazon Q Developer in my daily development workflow, significantly accelerating debugging and documentation creation. Networking Experience Interacting directly with AWS Principal Architects during the networking break was inspiring. Seeing how enterprise architects break down massive million-user banking architectures gave me clear insights into what it takes to become a professional Cloud Solutions Architect.

title: Create a gateway endpoint
content:
Open the Amazon VPC console In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint: You will see 6 existing VPC endpoints that support AWS Systems Manager (SSM). These endpoints were deployed automatically by the CloudFormation Templates for this workshop.
In the Create endpoint console: Specify name of the endpoint: s3-gwe In service category, choose AWS services In Services, type s3 in the search box and choose the service with type gateway For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. For Configure route tables, select the route table that is already associated with two subnets (note: this is not the main route table for the VPC, but a second route table created by CloudFormation). For Policy, leave the default option, Full Access, to allow full access to the service. You will deploy a VPC endpoint policy in a later lab module to demonstrate restricting access to S3 buckets based on policies. Do not add a tag to the VPC endpoint at this time. Click Create endpoint, then click x after receiving a successful creation message.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: Blog 2
content:
WHY CAN YOUR AWS BILL EXCEED A $10 BUDGET? This article was shared with the AWS Study Group community.
Published post: View the article on Facebook
Article Content AWS Budgets helps users monitor cloud spending and receive alerts when costs reach predefined thresholds. However, setting a $10 budget does not mean AWS will automatically stop services once that amount is reached.
To reduce unexpected expenses, users need to understand the difference between budget notifications and actual cost-control mechanisms.
Key Takeaways AWS Budgets: Monitors actual or forecasted costs and sends notifications through email or Amazon SNS when configured thresholds are reached. Budgets are not hard spending limits: AWS services may continue running and generating charges even after the budget is exceeded. Budgets Actions: Allows users to apply IAM policies or perform actions on specified EC2/RDS instances when budget thresholds are reached. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection: Uses Machine Learning to identify unusual spending patterns and notify users of potential cost anomalies. AWS Cost Explorer: Helps analyze expenses by service, Region, or usage type to identify the sources of unexpected costs. Cost Data Latency: Billing information is not updated continuously in real time, so actual spending may exceed the configured threshold before an alert is delivered. Practical Applications For learning accounts and testing environments, AWS Budgets, Cost Anomaly Detection, Cost Explorer, and Budgets Actions can be combined to monitor spending, detect unusual cost increases, and implement appropriate cost-control measures.
The key takeaway is that AWS Budgets does not guarantee that an account’s charges will never exceed the configured budget.

title: Proposal
content:
RELOOP An AI-assisted marketplace for used and broken electronics, built serverless on AWS 1. Executive Summary ReLoop is a web marketplace where people in Vietnam sell used or broken electronics (phones, laptops, monitors, components) to nearby repair shops, buyers and recyclers. It was built by AWSS3nt1n4L, a 5-person team in the AWS First Cloud Journey (FCAJ) program in Ho Chi Minh City, during a 12-week internship (14/09–04/12/2026). A seller uploads photos, and Amazon Bedrock pre-fills the listing. The listing then goes to every approved buyer whose branch service area (1–15 km) covers it, and the deal closes through a buyer quote or a price agreed in chat. On 08/11/2026 the dev environment had 14 registered accounts, 12 active listings from 7 sellers and about 31,000 API requests over the first month. The serverless design scales without re-architecture: Lambda concurrency is approved up to 1,000. The core services are CloudFront, AWS WAF, API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, S3, Cognito, Rekognition, Bedrock, EventBridge, CloudWatch and SNS. Guests can browse the market without an account. Signed-in users can chat and buy. Only Admin-approved partners can sell, and only Admin and Finance Admin can moderate content and handle invoices.
Team Member Role Kung Cẩm Thành Team Lead Hoàng Quốc Việt Tech Lead Trần Hoàng Quốc Trung Backend Engineer Nguyễn Duy Quang Frontend Engineer Nguyễn Anh Kỳ Cyber-security / Documentation 2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? The Global E-waste Monitor 2024 (UNITAR/ITU) reports that the world generated 62 million tonnes of e-waste in 2022, and only 22.3% was formally collected and recycled. The same report estimates that Vietnam generated about 516,000 tonnes (≈5.3 kg per person) in 2022. Owners of an old or broken device rarely know who will take it or what it is worth. Today they post on general classifieds sites or social groups, describe the device by hand, call shops one by one, and often get no answer. General marketplaces such as Chợ Tốt or Facebook Marketplace are built for any kind of goods. They do not:
match a listing to the shops whose service area covers the seller, show a price estimate from the buyer’s own pricing rules, keep a reputation record that rewards buyers who honour their quotes. Small repair shops face the same gap from the other side. They have no cheap channel to receive nearby devices that fit what they buy.
The Solution ReLoop runs the whole flow on managed AWS services. There are no servers to run.
Ingest: the browser uploads up to 6 photos per listing (JPEG/PNG/WebP, max 5 MB each) straight to Amazon S3 using presigned POST URLs. Amazon Rekognition checks every photo for unsafe content and reads any text in it. That text goes through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, so prompt-injection attempts are flagged for Admin review.
Processing: one AWS Lambda function (Node.js 22, arm64) serves 111 API routes behind Amazon API Gateway. It also calls itself asynchronously for slow work:
AI photo analysis with Kimi K3 on Bedrock, about 35 s per run; geohash + Haversine matching of listings to buyer branches. Amazon EventBridge triggers the same function every 15 minutes to expire listings, auto-complete transactions after 48 hours, send reminders and issue monthly invoices.
Storage: a single Amazon DynamoDB table (PK/SK + one GSI) stores every entity: users, partners, branches, pricing rules, listings, quotes, transactions, chats, reviews, invoices and audit logs. Writes are conditional, and money-related APIs require an Idempotency-Key. S3 lifecycle rules delete unused photos after 1 day and all photos after 90 days.
Interface: a React single-page app served from a private S3 bucket through Amazon CloudFront. It has a public market, a partner portal (2 tiers) and an Admin portal.
Security: Amazon Cognito handles sign-in with Admins / FinanceAdmins groups. API Gateway checks a JWT on every private route. Two AWS WAF web ACLs protect the site: one on CloudFront (managed rules + rate limits) and one on the Cognito user pool (login rate limit). A strict Content-Security-Policy is applied, and each IAM permission is limited to exactly what the code needs.
Compared with general classifieds, ReLoop adds AI-filled listings, service-area matching, rule-based price estimates, a two-step completion (seller confirms the final price, buyer accepts) and two-way reviews. ReLoop does not handle payment: buyer and seller pay each other in person at hand-over.
Benefits and Return on Investment Less manual input: AI suggests title, category, brand, model and condition from up to 3 photos. The seller only confirms or edits. A listing takes about 5 minutes by hand versus under 1 minute with AI (team estimate). Fewer unanswered listings: every new listing is matched automatically to all buyer branches in range, and listings within 5 km are ranked first. Reliability: state machines, conditional writes and idempotent background jobs keep listings, quotes and transactions consistent. 182 automated tests and an end-to-end smoke test run against AWS. Learning value: the team practised single-table DynamoDB design, event-driven Lambda, Bedrock structured output, Terraform IaC, WAF tuning and an automated pentest. Cost: about 18.70 USD/month (224.40 USD/year) at the current scale (section 6). 17.00 USD of that is AWS WAF, so without WAF the platform costs about 1.70 USD/month. Until 28/02/2027 the cost is covered by the account’s remaining credits (197.14 USD on 08/11/2026). Payback: revenue is 10,000 VND per completed transaction, paid by the seller. At an assumed rate of 1 USD ≈ 26,000 VND (approximate rate, November 2026), 18.70 USD ≈ 486,200 VND. The platform therefore breaks even at 49 completed transactions per month, or 5 per month without WAF. 3. Solution Architecture ReLoop is fully serverless in one region (ap-southeast-1):
All browser traffic passes AWS WAF and CloudFront. Static files come from a private S3 bucket, and /api/* is forwarded to an HTTP API with a secret origin header, so direct calls to API Gateway are rejected. One Lambda function holds the business logic. It calls DynamoDB, S3, Rekognition and Bedrock through small adapters, so the same code also runs locally on Node.js with in-memory storage. Sign-up and sign-in go directly from the browser to Cognito, protected by a second WAF. Logs and custom business metrics flow to CloudWatch, and alarms are sent to the Admin by SNS email. All infrastructure is defined in Terraform, with state stored in a versioned S3 bucket. Diagram source: static/images/2-Proposal/reloop-architecture.drawio (generated by diagram/make_architecture.py).
AWS Services Used Amazon CloudFront: serves the web app and routes /api/* to API Gateway. It adds CSP, HSTS and X-Frame-Options headers and returns a real 404 for missing static files. AWS WAF: 2 web ACLs. reloop-dev-web on CloudFront: 3 AWS managed rule groups plus 2 rate limits returning 429. The limits are 100 requests per minute per IP on the public API and 1,000 requests per minute per IP overall. reloop-dev-auth on Cognito: 300 sign-in attempts per 5 minutes per IP, plus IP reputation. Amazon S3: 3 buckets — web bundle (private, OAC), device photos (presigned POST/GET, tag-based lifecycle) and Terraform state (versioned). Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API): JWT authorizer on every private route; throttled at 20 requests/s with a burst of 50. AWS Lambda: reloop-dev-api, Node.js 22 on arm64 (Graviton) with 512 MB. It runs the API, the async AI/matching worker, the scheduled jobs and the Cognito pre sign-up trigger. Average duration is 144 ms; concurrency quota is 1,000. Amazon DynamoDB: one on-demand table with PK/SK and GSI1, PITR and TTL (notifications expire after 90 days). It holds about 5,600 items (2.4 MB). Amazon Cognito: user pool with email verification and groups Admins, FinanceAdmins, Partners and Owners. It has 14 users. Amazon Rekognition: moderation labels on every photo (rejects explicit content; borderline cases go to Admin) and text detection. Amazon Bedrock: Kimi K3 through the Converse API with tool choice, returning structured JSON. A Guardrail (Standard tier) screens AI input/output and text found in photos. Each user is capped at 20 analyses per day. Amazon EventBridge: 1 rule every 15 minutes that runs the background sweep. Amazon CloudWatch: logs kept 7 days, custom business metrics, 1 dashboard and 10 alarms (Lambda errors/throttles, API 5xx, p95 > 2 s, AI/job failures, unusual photo text, new disputes). Amazon SNS: sends alarm emails to Admin. AWS IAM: one execution role scoped to the core table, the photo prefix, the specific Bedrock model and Guardrail, Rekognition, self-invoke and logs. AWS Security Agent: automated black-box pentest of the dev site (3.63 task-hours on 08/11/2026). Component Design Edge / Client: a React 18 + TypeScript SPA (Vite) with Leaflet + OpenStreetMap for picking locations. Guests see the market. After sign-in, users see the partner portal (tier 1: individual sellers, max 3 open listings; tier 2: businesses with branches, pricing rules and quotes, max 10) or the Admin portal. Ingestion: POST /uploads/presign returns a 5-minute presigned POST, and the browser uploads the photo directly to S3. POST /uploads/moderate runs Rekognition and tags the photo moderation=passed. When a listing is created, its photos are tagged state=attached, so the lifecycle rule keeps them. Processing: an HTTP router handles JWT claims, idempotency keys and input checks. Domain state machines for Listing, Quote and Transaction allow only valid moves (for example, a transaction cancel takes effect after 5 minutes, and completion is auto-accepted after 48 hours). AI analysis and matching run as async self-invocations. A job runner keyed by “time buckets” finds due work without table scans. Storage: all access patterns are listed in backend/src/store/keys.ts; the code never scans the table. The market feed is partitioned by month and paginated with a validated cursor. Money is stored as integer VND. Web Interface: the public market, chat per listing (5-second polling) with price offers, the transaction drawer (schedule hand-over, adjust price, confirm, dispute) and reviews. User Management: Cognito sign-up with email verification. The pre sign-up trigger blocks one mailbox from opening several accounts through email aliases (name+1@…, dotted Gmail addresses). Admin approves partner applications, and Finance Admin issues and settles monthly invoices. If an invoice is more than 3 days overdue the seller cannot post new listings; after 7 days the account is locked. Monitoring: structured JSON logs, metric filters for business events, a dashboard (reloop-dev-overview), alarms to SNS email, and WAF logs to CloudWatch Logs with authorization and cookie fields redacted. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases Research & Architecture (28/09–09/10/2026): turned the 1,189-paragraph specification v1.0 into 45 written business decisions (QĐ-01 → QĐ-45), listed the DynamoDB access patterns, chose one Lambda behind an HTTP API, and wrote the first Terraform (Cognito, API Gateway, Lambda, S3/CloudFront). Cost Estimation & Feasibility (05/10–09/10/2026): dropped bank top-up/withdrawal (no bank API available) in favour of direct payment at hand-over; chose on-demand DynamoDB and arm64 Lambda; kept every AWS call behind interfaces so the team can develop locally without an AWS bill. Develop & First Deploy (05/10–23/10/2026): completed the full market flow on AWS (19/10), the two-tier partner model, quotes, chat offers, transactions, reviews, billing, moderation, and the smoke-aws.py end-to-end test (passing 22/10). Architecture Refinement (26/10–06/11/2026): rebuilt the whole UI from the product owner’s designs and added a new Admin portal; moved AI to Kimi K3 on Bedrock (28/10); ran 5 QA rounds (146 findings, 03/11); raised Lambda concurrency from 10 to 1,000; put AWS WAF on CloudFront and Cognito (06/11). Test, Harden & Hand Over (09/11–04/12/2026): pentest and fixes (week of 09/11); CSP enforcement; a single CI/CD deploy path with per-member IAM users; SES for email, AWS Budgets, load test, production environment; final documentation and demo. Technical Requirements Software: Node.js 22, TypeScript 5, React 18 + Vite 5, Leaflet, amazon-cognito-identity-js, AWS SDK v3, esbuild, Vitest; Python 3 for the AWS smoke test. Infrastructure as Code: Terraform ≥ 1.10 (AWS provider 6.x) with remote state in S3; infra/deploy.sh (build → terraform apply → upload web → CloudFront invalidation); AWS CLI ≥ 2.32. CI: GitHub Actions runs typecheck, 182 tests and the web build on every pull request. Hardware: none beyond the developers’ laptops. There are no devices on site. Skills: DynamoDB single-table modelling, IAM least privilege, Bedrock prompt and Guardrail design, WAF rule tuning, React, and testing with fakes for AWS services. 5. Timeline & Milestones Week Dates Deliverables Week 1 14/09–18/09 AWS foundations: account security, IAM, VPC, EC2; team onboarding Week 2 21/09–26/09 Serverless basics (S3, DynamoDB, Lambda, API Gateway); Buildrathon kickoff, ReLoop chosen (26/09) Week 3 28/09–02/10 Specification v1.0 turned into 45 business decisions (QĐ-01 → QĐ-45) and 58 open gaps; repo + CI; work split across the team Week 4 05/10–09/10 Architecture and DynamoDB access patterns (keys.ts); Cognito sign-in + React app; cost and feasibility choices Week 5 12/10–16/10 Photo upload to S3, Rekognition moderation, first AI listing analysis (Amazon Nova Pro) Week 6 19/10–24/10 Terraform dev environment; full market flow live on AWS (19/10); smoke test passing (22/10); EventBridge jobs; dashboard Week 7 26/10–30/10 New UI from PO designs (public site, partner portal, Admin portal); photo text + Guardrails; AI moved to Kimi K3 (28/10) Week 8 02/11–06/11 Background matching; 5 QA rounds (146 findings, 03/11); load test → Lambda concurrency 1,000; AI limit 20/day; WAF on CloudFront + Cognito (06/11) Week 9 09/11–13/11 AWS Security Agent pentest (7 findings, none high); fixes deployed; CSP enforced; SES for email; AWS Budgets alerts 50% / 80% Week 10 16/11–20/11 Load test re-run after throttling fix (20/s, burst 50); single CI/CD deploy path; IAM user per member; production environment Week 11 23/11–27/11 Terraform state migration; clean-up of unused resources; cost review Week 12 30/11–04/12 Final report, demo, hand-over documentation Post-launch 12/2026–02/2027 Run on the dev/prod environment within the credit window (until 28/02/2027); collect real usage data for the AI and matching 6. Budget Estimation The estimate is built from AWS public list prices for ap-southeast-1 (see AWS Pricing Calculator to reproduce it). The line-by-line estimate is in reloop-cost-estimate.csv.
Infrastructure Costs Region ap-southeast-1 (Singapore). The figures are based on real Cost Explorer and CloudWatch data from 26/09 to 08/11/2026: about 31,000 API requests and 14 users.
Service USD / month Assumption AWS WAF – CloudFront web ACL 10.00 1 web ACL (5.00) + 5 rules (5 × 1.00) + 0.60 per 1M requests AWS WAF – Cognito web ACL 7.00 1 web ACL (5.00) + 2 rules (2 × 1.00) Amazon Bedrock (Kimi K3 + Guardrails) 1.00 October usage (0.87 USD), capped at 20 analyses/user/day Amazon Rekognition 0.30 Moderation + text detection for ~70–100 photos/month Amazon DynamoDB (on-demand) 0.10 ~5,600 items, 2.4 MB, PITR on Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) 0.10 ~31,000 requests/month Amazon S3 0.05 Web bundle + photos (lifecycle 1/90 days) + Terraform state Miscellaneous (data transfer, other) 0.15 Buffer for small line items seen in October AWS Lambda 0.00 ~2,250 GB-s/month — Free Tier (1M requests + 400,000 GB-s) Amazon CloudFront 0.00 Free Tier (1 TB + 10M requests/month) Amazon Cognito 0.00 14 users — Free Tier up to 10,000 MAU Amazon CloudWatch + SNS + EventBridge 0.00 10 alarms, 1 dashboard, 7-day logs, email alerts, 1 schedule — Free Tier AWS Security Agent 0.00 Free trial (400 task-hours/month); 3.63 task-hours used Total per month 18.70 Total for 12 months 224.40 One-time hardware: 0 USD. Credits: the account is on the AWS Free plan with 197.14 USD of credits valid until 28/02/2027. That covers the roughly 3.7 months to that date (≈ 69 USD) at no cash cost. Optional saving: turning both WAF web ACLs off (waf_enabled, cognito_waf_enabled) lowers the bill to about 1.70 USD/month, but removes rate limiting and managed rules. Prices are AWS list prices for ap-southeast-1 in November 2026 and can change. Usage-based lines grow with traffic. 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Risk Impact Probability R1. Two machines deploy different code to the same Lambda (happened on 28/10/2026) High Medium R2. Credits run out or an unexpected charge appears (a Free-plan account is closed when credits are used up) High Low R3. Lambda/API throttling under bursts (load test: 80 parallel requests → 26% 5xx at concurrency 10) Medium Medium R4. AI misreads a device or is fed malicious text inside a photo Medium Medium R5. A security flaw in the public site or API High Low R6. Sellers and buyers close the deal off-platform to avoid the fee Medium High R7. Cognito’s default email limit (~50 emails/day) blocks sign-ups during a demo Medium Medium Mitigation Strategies R1: one deploy path (deploy.sh from a committed revision, moving to CI), an IAM user per member, and no root access keys. Check the live Lambda’s LastModified and CloudTrail before every deploy. R2: every paid feature is sized against the remaining credits before it is turned on, with hard caps (AI 20/day/user, pentest stopped at 3.5 task-hours). Add AWS Budgets alerts at 50% / 80%. R3: Lambda concurrency raised to 1,000; API Gateway throttle (20/s, burst 50) and WAF rate limits return 429 with Retry-After instead of failing. R4: AI only suggests and the seller confirms every field; the system stores the AI suggestion and the seller’s final value side by side. Guardrails and Rekognition flag suspicious photo text, and flagged listings wait for Admin review. R5: WAF managed rules, strict CSP, JWT on every private route, ownership checks on photo keys, and a pentest each release (latest: 7 findings, none high, fixes live on 08/11/2026). R6: a fee is charged when a listing is removed within 72 hours after a cancelled transaction, fee appeals go to Finance Admin, and repeat offenders are flagged. R7: move Cognito email to Amazon SES before public testing. Contingency Plans Bad deploy: redeploy the last good commit with deploy.sh. Terraform keeps everything else unchanged, and terraform plan shows the exact diff first. Cost spike: set waf_enabled=false / cognito_waf_enabled=false and lower the AI daily limit. Stop any Security Agent job with stop-pentest-job. Bedrock unavailable: AI is optional, so sellers fill in the form by hand and listings still go live. WAF or CSP blocks real users: change the rule/limit or the CSP in infra/waf.tf / infra/web.tf and apply. That takes one CloudFront update with no code release. Data issue: restore DynamoDB with PITR (up to 35 days). Photos can be re-uploaded by sellers. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements A complete, working marketplace on AWS: 111 API routes, 3 portals, 182 automated tests and an end-to-end smoke test passing on AWS. Infrastructure fully reproducible from Terraform in one command, at about 18.70 USD/month. The variable part (Lambda, DynamoDB, API Gateway, S3) costs under 1 USD/month at current traffic. Measurable security baseline: WAF on both entry points, strict CSP, and a pentest with 7 findings, none high, all fixable ones fixed. Response time: average Lambda duration of 144 ms, with an alarm if p95 goes above 2 s. Long-term Value Every listing stores the AI suggestion next to the seller’s final value. Over time this becomes labelled data for evaluating or fine-tuning device recognition. The adapter design (Table, ImageStore, Analyzer, AuthProvider) lets the team swap or add services, such as SES email, WebSocket chat or a bank payment API, without touching the business logic. The same Terraform and deploy script can create a production stack or a stack for another city. The geohash matching works anywhere. Shops and recyclers gain a steady, local channel for used devices. That moves more devices into reuse and formal recycling instead of household storage.

WHY DOES AN API STILL NEED THROTTLING WHEN AWS WAF IS ALREADY ENABLED? This article was shared with the AWS Study Group community.
Published post: View the article on Facebook
Article Content When an API receives a large volume of requests, AWS WAF alone may not be sufficient to control all traffic reaching the backend. AWS WAF and API Gateway Throttling serve different purposes: one filters suspicious traffic early, while the other controls request rates before backend execution.
The example architecture follows Client → Amazon CloudFront (AWS WAF) → Amazon API Gateway → AWS Lambda, with Amazon CloudWatch providing monitoring across the protection layers.
Key Takeaways AWS WAF Rate-based Rules: Monitor request frequency by IP address or other configured aggregation criteria to limit unusual traffic before it reaches API Gateway. Scope-down Statements: Allow rate-based rules to target specific endpoints, such as /api/search, instead of the entire website. API Gateway Throttling: Uses Rate Limits and Burst Limits to control request traffic and reduce pressure on AWS Lambda. HTTP 403 and 429: AWS WAF returns HTTP 403 by default for blocked requests, while API Gateway may return HTTP 429 when throttling limits are exceeded. Direct API Access: If the default execute-api endpoint remains accessible, clients may bypass the WAF protection associated with CloudFront. CloudWatch Monitoring: Combines WAF logs, API Gateway metrics/access logs, and Lambda metrics to identify where requests are blocked or processed. Practical Applications For public APIs, combining AWS WAF with API Gateway Throttling helps limit unusual traffic, manage backend workloads, and reduce the risk of disrupting legitimate users.
A recommended approach is to test WAF Rate-based Rules using the Count action before switching to Block. Direct access to API Gateway should also be reviewed, while logs and metrics are monitored to verify the effectiveness of each protection layer.

title: Blog 4
content:
AMAZON BEDROCK: CONTROLLING REQUESTS AND TOKEN USAGE BEFORE COSTS INCREASE This article was shared with the AWS Study Group community.
Published post: View the article on Facebook
Article Content When deploying Generative AI applications with Amazon Bedrock, limiting the number of API requests alone is not sufficient for effective cost management. Even valid requests can consume large numbers of tokens due to long prompts or extensive outputs, especially in multi-tenant applications.
To reduce unexpected expenses, a layered architecture can combine Amazon CloudFront, AWS WAF, API Gateway, AWS Lambda, DynamoDB, and Amazon Bedrock, supported by monitoring and usage analytics services.
Key Takeaways AWS WAF and Amazon CloudFront: Filter unusual traffic at the edge using Rate-based Rules, reducing unnecessary requests before they reach the application. Amazon API Gateway: Provides authentication, authorization, and throttling through Rate Limits and Burst Limits to control incoming traffic. AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB: Implement a Quota Controller to enforce per-tenant request or token limits before invoking Bedrock. Atomic and Conditional Updates: Help maintain accurate quota records when multiple requests are processed concurrently. Token Usage Tracking: Estimates token consumption before inference and reconciles it with actual usage after Bedrock returns a response. Amazon CloudWatch and SNS: Monitor model invocations, input/output tokens, and send notifications when usage exceeds configured thresholds. Amazon S3 and Athena: Store and analyze usage data by tenant, model, or time period to support more detailed cost management. Practical Applications This architecture is useful for AI applications serving multiple users or tenants, where individual usage limits are needed to reduce unexpected costs caused by repeated requests or excessive token consumption.
For smaller applications, Lambda, DynamoDB, and CloudWatch can provide a practical starting point. S3 and Athena can be introduced later when more advanced usage analysis is required.
Application-level quotas must also account for concurrent requests, retries, and differences between estimated and actual token usage. These controls help reduce unexpected consumption but do not guarantee an absolute spending limit.

title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.

Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. title: Workshop
content:
Secure Hybrid Access to S3 using VPC Endpoints Overview AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity to AWS services from Amazon VPCs and your on-premises networks without exposing your traffic to the Public Internet.
In this comprehensive hands-on workshop, you will learn how to design, configure, and validate VPC endpoints that allow hybrid cloud workloads to interact with AWS services with enterprise-grade isolation and zero internet egress dependencies.
You will implement and evaluate two distinct types of VPC endpoints for Amazon S3:
Gateway VPC Endpoint: Directs traffic from subnets to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB via private AWS internal routing. Traffic is routed using VPC Route Table prefix lists at zero additional service cost. Interface VPC Endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink): Provisions elastic network interfaces (ENIs) with private IP addresses inside your VPC subnets, enabling seamless, secure access from on-premises datacenters over VPN or AWS Direct Connect. title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
Thoughts, Reflections & Constructive Feedback The 12-week journey with the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) bootcamp has been one of the most rewarding and formative experiences of my academic life. Beyond the technical knowledge gained, this program transformed how I approach engineering problems, collaborate with peers, and navigate real-world cloud challenges.
Below are my honest reflections and constructive recommendations for future cohort iterations:
Detailed Program Evaluation 1. Learning Environment & Culture Impression: The learning atmosphere is exceptionally welcoming, energetic, and supportive. From day one, senior mentors and team coordinators treated interns as colleagues rather than mere students. Positive Highlight: The active discussion channels on Slack/Facebook Group provided rapid assistance whenever someone ran into tricky IAM permissions or VPC peering bugs, even late in the evening. Suggestion: It would be fantastic to incorporate more informal team bonding activities or virtual coffee chats to foster even deeper connections among participants across different university campuses. 2. Quality of Mentorship & Leadership Guidance Impression: The mentors are deeply knowledgeable, patient, and inspiring. The “Teach to Fish” Philosophy: Instead of simply handing out quick code snippets to fix our errors, mentors consistently asked probing questions (e.g., “What does CloudWatch Logs show? What is the HTTP status code returning?”), training us to develop autonomous troubleshooting reflexes. Suggestion: Scheduling bi-weekly 1-on-1 progress check-ins with mentors would be immensely valuable for interns to receive targeted individual feedback on personal career roadmaps. 3. Alignment with University Curriculum & Industry Demands Impression: The curriculum serves as the perfect bridge between university computer science foundations (Operating Systems, Computer Networks, Database Systems) and modern industrial cloud engineering. Value: Theoretical knowledge of routing protocols or relational schemas came alive when we actually configured Route Tables, NAT Gateways, and Multi-AZ RDS clusters in live AWS production environments. 4. Growth in Soft Skills & Engineering Maturity Key Gains: In addition to technical proficiency, the mandatory requirements to write weekly worklogs, publish community blogs, and present capstone workshops drastically enhanced my technical writing, storytelling, and public speaking abilities. Key Questions & Retrospective Thoughts What was the most satisfying moment during your internship? The most thrilling milestone was the moment my automated CI/CD pipeline triggered by a Git push successfully tested, built, and deployed the entire multi-region architecture without a single manual console click. Seeing theory transform into working, highly available cloud infrastructure was unforgettable.
What could the program improve for upcoming cohorts? Curated Lab Budget Credits: Providing dedicated AWS credit vouchers or sandbox accounts with pre-allocated budgets would give students even greater peace of mind to experiment boldly with heavier services like Amazon OpenSearch or Amazon EKS without worrying about personal credit card charges. Architecture Whiteboard Challenges: Adding interactive whiteboard architecture design sessions in small teams would sharpen rapid system design interview skills. Would you recommend this program to fellow university students? Absolutely 100% yes. I have already encouraged several promising juniors in my university’s IT faculty to apply for upcoming cohorts. The First Cloud AI Journey provides practical, resume-defining engineering skills that simply cannot be acquired through textbooks alone.
Sincere Words of Appreciation I would like to express my heartfelt gratitude to the entire First Cloud AI Journey leadership team, AWS Vietnam mentors, and my wonderful fellow interns. Thank you for creating an extraordinary learning platform, for your selfless guidance, and for empowering young students to step boldly into the cloud computing era!
